overview: The Chandelas built a powerful kingdom in Bundelkhand, with Khajuraho, Mahoba and Kalinjar among its important centres. The map’s 1100 to 1200 span selects one late phase: the dynasty and much of its celebrated temple building were older. Its broad outline is an approximation, not a surveyed frontier.

periods.title: Earlier rise
periods.summary: Chandela rulers emerged from the Pratihara political world. Yashovarman captured Kalinjar and commissioned the Lakshmana temple.

periods.title: Great temple-building age
periods.summary: Khajuraho’s principal architectural flowering accompanied the dynasty’s tenth- and eleventh-century strength.

periods.title: Recovery and later patrons
periods.summary: Kirtivarman restored power; Madanavarman and Paramardi sustained a courtly and religious culture into the twelfth century.

periods.title: Conquest and regional survival
periods.summary: Aibak defeated Paramardi around 1202-1203. Later Chandela rulers continued, although the great kingdom’s power diminished.

items.text: Kalinjar was a strategic hill fortress as well as a sacred place. Yashovarman’s acquisition of it in the tenth century strengthened a dynasty growing beyond its earlier subordinate position. Temple patronage and military authority developed together.

Government depended on experienced officials. The twelfth-century Mau inscription traces a family serving successive kings and records a minister’s temple and tank building. Its account of hereditary service also praises practical skill and judgment: a royal title alone did not run the kingdom.

At Mahoba, lakes were created by placing substantial embankments across shallow valleys. The district handbook describes a linked landscape of tanks around the town. Managing a valley’s water was an achievement on a very different scale from carving a necklace on a statue.

Madan Sagar is associated with Madanavarman, who ruled around 1128 to 1165, directly within this map record’s period. Rahila Sagar and Kirat Sagar commemorate earlier rulers. The landscape preserves several generations of building, not a single king’s afternoon project.

An Indian Museum sculpture from tenth- or eleventh-century Khajuraho shows a mother holding a child in both hands beneath a bower. This affectionate subject belongs beside the gods and kings when imagining the culture’s artistic interests.

The same figure has her hair swept behind her ears and gathered into a large bow with a flower. Her thin garment reaches towards her anklets. The sculptor spent care on small choices of dress and grooming as well as the mother’s pose.

A sandstone couple from eleventh-century Khajuraho, now in Cleveland, represents idealized lovers. The museum explains such imagery as a wish for birth, prosperity and abundance at a sacred building. These images have religious meanings as well as showing human affection.

A Khajuraho sculpture depicts a woman using a cone-shaped stylus. Archaeologist George Dales suggested the surface might be a wax tablet. The image offers a glimpse of writing equipment and an educated female figure, although it cannot tell us how many girls attended lessons.

Khajuraho’s carvings include teachers with disciples, dancers, musicians and domestic scenes. A temple exterior could present many kinds of human activity alongside divine beings. Learning and performance had a place in this visual world, even though stone scenes do not describe a school timetable.

Water could also be approached on foot: the handbook describes granite steps and ghats at Kirat Sagar. These surviving features make the lakes more than distant scenery. They connect the water’s edge with the spaces where people moved around the town.

sections.title: Building, giving and leaving words behind

items.text: Khajuraho’s major temples stand on raised platforms. A visitor moves through a porch, hall and vestibule towards the sanctuary; some buildings provide a route around that inner room. Architecture guides movement as carefully as it frames a view.

The main spire rises among smaller spires, creating a mountain-like silhouette. Sandstone walls carry rich sculpture, while projecting windows and subsidiary shrines enliven the building. Hindu and Jain temples survive within the same monumental landscape.

Pahilla’s temple record lists gardens, including a mango garden, among his gifts. Its date refers back to the tenth century, but Kielhorn judged the surviving lettering a later re-engraving. The gift connected religious support with cultivated land and responsibilities extending beyond the donor’s lifetime.

Written Sanskrit: “नमो भगवते वासुदेवाय” (namo bhagavate vāsudevāya), “Adoration to the holy Vasudeva.” This invocation closes the Lakshmana temple inscription dated Vikrama year 1011, conventionally 954 CE. It is an earlier Chandela witness, reproduced here in modern Devanagari type, before the map’s 1100 start.

That inscription also names its poet Madhava and its writer Jaddha, a Sanskrit-knowing writer of legal documents. The monument preserves traces of specialized literary and scribal work as well as royal praise.

ASI excavations reported for 1988-89 uncovered damaged brick platforms, a shrine and traces of flooring at Khajuraho. The excavators separated earlier Post-Gupta or Pratihara occupation from a Chandela phase. Standing sandstone temples are only part of the site’s longer building history.

The same excavation recovered red and black pottery, terracotta beads and animal figures, iron objects and a copper ring. Some architectural pieces carried masons’ marks. The report does not assign every small object to one phase, so they reveal the excavated site’s activities without supplying a precise Chandela household inventory.

Later Chandela patronage still had practical effects. A thirteenth-century Ajaygarh record describes Queen Kalyanadevi’s well, water-distribution hall and tank at Nandipura. Women could appear in inscriptions as patrons of public works, as well as in sculpture as mothers or divine figures.

ending.text: The map’s 1200 cutoff is not the dynasty’s disappearance. Aibak’s conquest around 1202-1203 weakened Chandela power, but subsequent rulers survived regionally through the thirteenth century. Their political reach changed while temples, inscriptions and waterworks remained.
